extracted.intended_audience: grant seekers (nonprofit organizations, government entities, individual grant writers)
extracted.subtask_description: A step-by-step framework for developing competitive grant proposals for government, foundation, and corporate funders, covering planning, design, budgets, evaluation, submission, and follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Assessment (organizational fit & readiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Who am I? (and what in the world do I want to do?)" — Identify your organization's mission, capacity, fit for funders; assess readiness for grant funding; match grants to organizational priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mission alignment with the grant opportunity, internal capacity to implement and manage a grant, and whether pursuing grant funding matches organizational strategic priorities. Use this to screen prospects and avoid pursuing misfits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant Fundamentals (types, funder ecosystem, cycles)
rubrics_metrics.description: "What is a grant, and where do I get one?" — Understand different types of grants (project, operating, capital, capacity), the funder ecosystem (government, foundation, corporate), and grant cycles and deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the differences in expectations and rules across funder types (e.g., foundations vs. federal grants), track calendars and deadlines, and choose grant types that fit project scope and organizational needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying Funders (research & prospecting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Funder research strategies including use of Foundation Center / Candid resources, federal grant databases, and building a prospect list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically research prospects using databases and directories, prioritize funders whose interests match your program, and maintain a prospect list to plan outreach and submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading and Decoding RFPs (compliance & scoring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the funder's exact instructions, identify scoring criteria, and build a compliance checklist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully parse RFPs to extract required elements and scoring rubrics; construct a compliance checklist to ensure all format, attachment, and content requirements are met. Noncompliance can lead to disqualification regardless of program quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-Proposal Activities (LOIs, concept papers, relationships)
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities before full proposal submission: letters of inquiry (LOI), concept papers, and building relationships with program officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use LOIs/concept papers to test funder interest; cultivate relationships with program officers for insights into priorities and fit; be strategic about early communications to improve chances of invitation or guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project Design (logic models & backward design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design projects using logic models, theory of change, and backward design from outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with desired outcomes and work backwards to activities and inputs. Use logic models/theory of change to show causal links between resources, activities, outputs, and outcomes; align design with evidence and funder priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need Statement (documenting the problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Identifying and documenting the need: what problem will a grant fix?" — Use local data and statistics, national context, characterize affected population, explain why now/urgency, and avoid deficit framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific, evidence-based description of the problem with relevant local and broader context; describe who is affected and why the intervention is timely; frame needs respectfully (avoid solely deficit language) and connect need to the proposed solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals and Objectives (SMART objectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: "What do you hope to achieve if you get the money?" — Distinguish goals (broad aspirational statements) from objectives; make objectives SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Differentiate process objectives vs. outcome objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a small set of measurable objectives tied to timelines and baselines. Include both process (implementation) metrics and outcome (impact) metrics and ensure each objective maps to activities and evaluation methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods/Activities (implementation detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a detailed program description including staffing and roles, timeline (Gantt charts often helpful), and implementation steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe who will do what, when, and how; include realistic timelines and milestones; justify staffing and roles; present clear workflow and operational details so reviewers can assess feasibility and capacity to deliver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Change / Logic Model (linking inputs to impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use inputs → activities → outputs → outcomes → impact framework; provide a visual representation of your program and connect evidence to design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the causal pathway from resources to long-term impact. Use visuals to clarify relationships and explicitly cite evidence or prior findings that support the design choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation Plan (process & outcome evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: "How can you be sure if your program worked?" — Include process evaluation (implementation fidelity) and outcome evaluation (results); decide internal vs. external evaluator; provide data collection plan and reporting timeline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify measurable indicators for objectives, data sources, instruments, timing, responsible parties, and analysis plans. Describe whether evaluation is formative/summative and whether an external evaluator will be used to strengthen credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget and Budget Narrative (cost realism & justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: "How much will it cost, and is the cost reasonable?" — Distinguish direct vs. indirect costs; include personnel, fringe benefits, travel, equipment, supplies, subcontracts/consultants, other direct costs, and provide detailed justification for each line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure budget aligns with activities and staffing and that costs are reasonable and allowable per funder rules. Provide clear line-item explanations in the narrative tied to program tasks; include calculations, rates, and any matching or in-kind contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustainability (post-grant continuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: "How will you continue the program when the grant funds run out?" — Describe diversified funding strategy, built-in revenue (fees, subscriptions), institutional commitment, reduced cost over time, and spinoffs/replication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate realistic plans for sustaining activities beyond the grant period, including other funding sources, earned income, organizational support, and strategies to reduce reliance on a single funder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover Letter and Executive Summary (elevator pitch)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cover letter/executive summary is the "elevator pitch" of your proposal; it is often the most important section for many funders and should be written last but appears first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a concise, compelling summary that highlights need, proposed solution, key outcomes, organizational credibility, and budget snapshot. Tailor tone and emphasis to the funder's priorities and reviewer expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission and Follow-Up (compliance & stewardship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow submission instructions exactly, confirm receipt, respond to clarification requests, prepare for site visits, and conduct post-decision follow-up whether funded or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use checklists to ensure full compliance with submission requirements; document submissions and communications; debrief and follow up with funders after decisions to build relationships and learn from reviewer feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational Elements of a Strong Proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Core qualities that make proposals competitive: clear, compelling need; strong organizational fit; realistic and detailed plan; capable team; reasonable budget; believable sustainability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each proposal element (need, design, team, budget, sustainability) is coherent and mutually reinforcing. Reviewers look for alignment among these elements and for credibility demonstrated through evidence and realistic planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice and Style (tone and clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred writing style: professional but human; specific not vague; confident not boastful; active not passive; fact-based not anecdotal alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt clear, direct prose that balances professionalism with accessibility. Use active voice, precise language, and evidence to support claims. Avoid excessive jargon, unsupported anecdotes, or overstated claims that undermine credibility.
